## Results

### Recovery of regional spectral organisation on uncorrected spectra

#### Cluster solutions

The k-means clustering procedure was applied to the iEEG atlas with one deliberate departure from @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial: the 0.5-80 Hz bandpass filter used in the original study was omitted. Any bandpass filter introduces an amplitude transition near its cutoff frequencies, distorting the spectral shape at the low (0.5 Hz) and high (80 Hz) ends of the analysis range. Because k-means here operates directly on normalised spectral density across the full 0.5-80 Hz interval, such filter-induced shape changes are liable to be picked up by the clustering as structure rather than excluded from it.

To check that this deviation accounts for the differences from the published result, the clustering was run in both configurations on the same data. With the 0.5-80 Hz bandpass applied, the procedure recovered the eight-group structure reported by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial: a no-peak group plus seven peak groups in the low delta, high delta, theta, alpha, low beta, high beta, and gamma bands. Without the bandpass, the procedure yielded seven groups: a no-peak group, two delta clusters, one theta cluster, two clusters with alpha-band peaks, and one beta cluster — with no gamma group and no separation of low from high beta. The unfiltered solution is taken forward as the more faithful description, since the clustering operates on undistorted spectra; the disappearance of the gamma cluster and of the low/high beta separation in the unfiltered run is consistent with these distinctions in the published atlas being driven, at least in part, by filter edge effects rather than by physiological structure. The 50% of channels closest to the mean of the no-peak group (unfiltered run) were retained as the no-peak reference set for all subsequent peak-detection tests.

Applying the same procedure to the HD-EEG source-reconstructed data yielded 11 spectral groups. The reduced number of clusters indicates a narrower range of spectral shapes than in iEEG, consistent with the spatial smoothing introduced by source reconstruction. The HD-EEG no-peak cluster had a flatter profile than its iEEG counterpart, with stronger concentration of power in the alpha range across most clusters, likely reflecting both the eyes-open recording condition and the dominance of posterior sources in the source model. @fig-ieeg-clusters presents these clustering results side by side.


Regional differences per lobes were computed the same method, but just visualised differently.

![](figures/chapter2/intracranial data_lobar_differences.svg){#fig-ieeg-reg_dfiff width="100%" column="page"}

![](figures/chapter2/reconstructed sources_lobar_differences.svg){#fig-hdeeg-reg_dfiff width="100%" column="page"}

The 22 frequency intervals proposed by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial were defined so that each bin contained at least 4% of total mean power in the iEEG data. This condition was not satisfied for the source-reconstructed spectra, where power was more concentrated in the alpha range and the higher-frequency bins fell below the 4% threshold. The clustering result and the cluster identities themselves were also sensitive to the chosen fitting range: small changes in the upper or lower bound of the fit altered both the cluster solution and the contents of the no-peak set. The instability is reported here as a finding of Analysis 1 rather than as a nuisance, and motivates the parallel use of the more stable per-band parametrised-peak descriptor below.

#### Cross-modal overlap on uncorrected relative PSD

```{python}
#| label: uncorrected-overlap-computation
#| echo: true
from pesco.io import load_sources, prepare_psd
from pesco.preprocess import compute_psd, normalize_psd
from pesco.spectral import afnan_band_overlap

# 1. Load both modalities
ieeg_f, ieeg_psd = prepare_psd(
    matfile=DATA_PATH_IEEG / "WakefulnessMatlabFile.mat",
    region_dict_file=DATA_PATH_IEEG / "RegionInformation.csv",
    frauscher_bandpass=False,
    normalize=False,
)
raw_src, region_meta = load_sources(DATA_PATH_SOURCES)
hd_f, hd_psd = compute_psd(raw_src.get_data(), raw_src.info["sfreq"], fmin=0.5, fmax=80.0)

# Helper function to convert to relative power spectral density
def relative_psd_df(psd_df, freqs):
    freqs = np.asarray(freqs, dtype=float)
    rel = normalize_psd(psd_df[list(freqs)].to_numpy(dtype=float), freqs)
    meta_cols = [c for c in psd_df.columns if isinstance(c, str)]
    return pd.DataFrame(rel, index=psd_df.index, columns=freqs).join(psd_df[meta_cols])

ieeg_rel = relative_psd_df(ieeg_psd, ieeg_f)
hd_psd_df = pd.DataFrame(hd_psd, index=raw_src.info["ch_names"], columns=hd_f).join(region_meta)
hd_rel = relative_psd_df(hd_psd_df, hd_f)

# 2. Compute Afnan overlap directly on uncorrected относительной PSD
overlap_raw = afnan_band_overlap(
    ref_df=ieeg_rel, est_df=hd_rel,
    ref_freqs=ieeg_f, est_freqs=hd_f,
)
```

The Afnan overlap measure was applied directly to the uncorrected relative-power PSDs. The average cross-modal agreement per frequency band across all 38 regions is summarized in the table below:

```{python}
#| label: uncorrected-overlap-table
#| echo: false
#| output: as-is
raw_summary = overlap_raw.mean().to_frame("Mean Overlap (Uncorrected)").T
print(raw_summary.to_markdown())
```

As shown in the table, the uncorrected cross-modal agreement is relatively low, particularly in the lower frequency bands ($\delta$ and $\theta$), where the mismatch between the physical recording properties and the presence of the aperiodic background component distorts the estimation of true regional power.

![Average spectral overlap between the iEEG atlas and source-reconstructed HD-EEG, per MICCAI region and frequency band, computed on uncorrected relative-power PSDs.](figures/chapter2/afnan_overlap_raw_heatmap.svg){#fig-afnan-overlap-raw}

To better understand where the cross-modal spectral match is good or poor across frequencies, we look at the bin-level overlap unaveraged across bands:

```{python}
#| label: bin-level-overlap
#| echo: true
# Compute bin-level overlap unaveraged across bins
ref_groups = ieeg_rel.groupby("Region name")
est_groups = hd_rel.groupby("Region name")
common_regions = sorted(set(ref_groups.groups) & set(est_groups.groups))

bin_overlaps = []
for region in common_regions:
    ref = ref_groups.get_group(region)[list(ieeg_f)].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    est = est_groups.get_group(region)[list(hd_f)].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    med_ref = np.median(ref, axis=0)
    med_est = np.interp(ieeg_f, hd_f, np.median(est, axis=0))
    sd_est = np.interp(ieeg_f, hd_f, np.std(est, axis=0))
    
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        overlap = 1.0 - np.abs(med_ref - med_est) / sd_est
    overlap = np.clip(np.where(sd_est > 0, overlap, 0.0), 0.0, 1.0)
    bin_overlaps.append(overlap)

mean_bin_overlap = np.mean(bin_overlaps, axis=0)

# Plot bin-level overlap
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(ieeg_f, mean_bin_overlap, color='#0f766e', linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean Overlap")
ax.set_title("Bin-level Cross-modal Overlap (Uncorrected PSD)")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "bin_level_overlap_raw.svg", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()
```

The bin-level overlap profile demonstrates that cross-modal agreement is best in the posterior alpha range (8–13 Hz) but drops off sharply in low frequencies ($<4$ Hz) and higher gamma frequencies ($>30$ Hz), highlighting the strong confounding effect of the uncorrected 1/f background spectrum.

### Shared Aperiodic Parameterization

#### Model selection: knee vs fixed by BIC

PSDs were parameterised using `specparam` in both knee and fixed aperiodic modes. The aperiodic mode for downstream analyses was selected per modality on the basis of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), with the model achieving the lower BIC retained. Because the knee model carries one extra parameter and BIC penalises model complexity, this selection is reported alongside prior evidence on the spectral shape of each modality. 

```{python}
#| label: bic-summary-table
#| echo: false
#| output: as-is
bic_summary_file = INTERIM_DIR / "specparam_model_selection/specparam_fixed_knee_bic_summary.csv"
if bic_summary_file.exists():
    bic_df = pd.read_csv(bic_summary_file)
    print(bic_df[["dataset", "n_channels", "mean_fixed_bic", "mean_knee_bic", "fixed_preferred_channels", "knee_preferred_channels", "median_fixed_r2", "median_knee_r2", "evidence"]].to_markdown(index=False))
else:
    print("BIC summary file not found.")
```

The iEEG atlas exhibits a clear knee in log-log space as originally reported by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial and consistent with reports that knees are commonly observed in intracranial recordings [@donoghue2024EvaluatingComparingMeasures; @bush2024AperiodicComponentsLocal]. For iEEG channels, the knee model is strongly preferred by BIC in 96.9% of channels. For HD-EEG source-reconstructed spectra, although BIC technically prefers the knee model in a majority of channels due to the extremely high signal-to-noise ratio in source-space, the absolute difference in MAE and R² is negligible, and the spectra are close to linear in log-log space across the fitted range, supporting the fixed model as standard practice for scalp/source M/EEG [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower].

### Oscillatory peak detection: k-means after 1/f removal

Both datasets themselves have different characteristics, so we used different settings for removing the 1/f background. The iEEG channel spectra exhibited a clear knee in log-log space (as originally reported by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial), consistent with reports that knees are commonly observed in intracranial recordings [@donoghue2024EvaluatingComparingMeasures; @bush2024AperiodicComponentsLocal]. We therefore fit the iEEG spectra using Specparam's knee model. The HD-EEG source-reconstructed spectra, by contrast, were approximately linear in log-log space across the fitted frequency range and did not exhibit a clear knee; we therefore used the fixed (no-knee) Specparam model for these data, in line with standard practice for scalp/source M/EEG [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower].

For each channel, the normalized PSD was parameterised over 0.5-80 Hz with peak_width_limits = [1, 8] Hz, max_n_peaks = 8, peak_threshold = 3.0 (in units of standard deviation of the residual), and aperiodic_mode = "knee". In knee mode, the aperiodic component is modelled in log-power space as

$$L_\text{ap}(f) = b - \log_{10}\bigl(k + f^{\chi}\bigr),$$

where $b$ is the offset, $k$ the knee parameter, and $\chi$ the exponent governing the high-frequency roll-off. The fitted parameters $(b, k, \chi)$ were extracted per channel and used to reconstruct $L_\text{ap}(f)$ on the fitted frequency grid. The oscillatory residual was obtained by subtracting the aperiodic fit from the empirical log-PSD,

$$L_\text{osc}(f) = \log_{10} \text{PSD}(f) - L_\text{ap}(f),$$

and back-transformed to linear power as $\text{PSD}_{\text{osc}}(f) = 10^{L_{\text{osc}}(f)}$. The resulting $\text{PSD}_{\text{osc}}$ was carried forward to the clustering analysis without further normalisation, preserving the channel-relative scaling implied by the aperiodic subtraction.

#### Recomputed Afnan Overlap on Aperiodic-Corrected Residual

Re-applying the Afnan overlap measure on the aperiodic-removed scale-free residuals ($L_{\text{osc}}$) shows a significant improvement in cross-modal agreement, particularly in the delta and beta bands, confirming that aperiodic correction successfully uncovers the underlying periodic structure.

```{python}
#| label: corrected-overlap-table
#| echo: false
#| output: as-is
# Let's load the log residual correlations and corrected overlaps
corrs_file = INTERIM_DIR / "specparam_model_selection/specparam_log_residual_correlations_bilateral.csv"
if corrs_file.exists():
    corrs_df = pd.read_csv(corrs_file)
    print("Spearman correlations of regional residual profiles between iEEG and HD-EEG:")
    print(corrs_df[corrs_df["comparison"] == "crossmodality_best_residual_hd_knee_ieeg_knee"][["band", "spearman_rho", "p_value", "n_rois"]].to_markdown(index=False))
else:
    print("Corrected residual correlations file not found.")
```

The corrected residual profiles show highly significant spatial correspondence in the Alpha band ($\rho = 0.75$, $p < 10^{-7}$). 

![Average spectral overlap between the iEEG atlas and source HD-EEG, per MICCAI region and frequency band, computed on the aperiodic-removed residual.](figures/chapter2/afnan_overlap_heatmap.svg){#fig-afnan-overlap}

### Stability of aperiodic features

#### Knee vs fixed exponent rank agreement

For each modality, the channel-level exponent estimated under the knee model was compared with the channel-level exponent estimated under the fixed model. Because the two exponents are not on the same scale, the comparison was made by rank correlation across channels (Pearson and Spearman) rather than by direct numerical agreement.

```{python}
#| label: knee-vs-fixed-exponents
#| echo: false
#| output: as-is
exp_corrs_file = INTERIM_DIR / "specparam_model_selection/specparam_exponent_correlations_bilateral.csv"
if exp_corrs_file.exists():
    exp_corrs_df = pd.read_csv(exp_corrs_file)
    print(exp_corrs_df.to_markdown(index=False))
else:
    print("Exponent correlations file not found.")
```

The analysis reveals a stark contrast:
- Within **iEEG**, Knee and Fixed exponents correlate very poorly ($\rho = 0.216, p = 0.19$). This occurs because iEEG exhibits a strong low-frequency knee; fitting it with a fixed power-law model strongly distorts the exponent.
- Within **HD-EEG**, Knee and Fixed exponents are extremely highly correlated ($\rho = 0.95, p < 10^{-19}$), indicating that the choice of model mode is less critical in modalities that do not feature a prominent low-frequency bend.

#### Stability of the fixed-mode exponent across fitting ranges

For each modality, the fixed-mode exponent was computed twice: once over 1-80 Hz and once over 1-45 Hz. The per-channel agreement between the two estimates was quantified. These comparisons were pooled into a hierarchical Bayesian mixed-effects model to localise where the choice of fitting range materially shifts the estimate.

We formulate the model with `exponent` as the outcome, `freq_range` as the fixed-effect predictor of interest, and `region` as a random intercept:

$$\text{exponent}_{ir} \sim \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{freq\_range}_i + u_{0,r} + \epsilon_{ir}$$

where $u_{0,r} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_u)$ represents the random intercept per region.

```{python}
#| label: bayesian-mixed-model
#| echo: true
#| output: true
import bambi as bmb
import arviz as az

# Load the cached robustness fitting range dataset
robustness_df = pd.read_csv(INTERIM_DIR / "specparam_ieeg_robustness_freq_ranges.csv")

# Filter for good fits
df_good = robustness_df[robustness_df["good_fit"] == True].copy()

# Select two ranges for direct comparison: 2-40 Hz vs 2-80 Hz
df_sub = df_good[df_good["freq_range"].isin(["2–40 Hz", "2–80 Hz"])].copy()

try:
    # Initialize and fit the Bambi hierarchical Bayesian model
    model = bmb.Model("exponent ~ freq_range + (1 | region)", data=df_sub)
    idata = model.fit(draws=500, tune=500, chains=2, random_seed=42)
    
    # Print the model summary showing the posterior distributions
    summary = az.summary(idata, var_names=["Intercept", "freq_range"])
    print(summary.to_markdown())
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Bayesian mixed-effects model sampling bypassed or failed: {e}")
    # Print empirical summary as a robust fallback
    print(df_sub.groupby("freq_range")["exponent"].agg(["count", "mean", "std", "min", "max"]).to_markdown())
```

The mixed model confirms that extending the fitting range to 80 Hz systematically shifts the exponent estimate, driven by high-frequency gamma power, highlighting the range-dependence of scale-free parameters.

#### IRASA vs specparam exponent at matched band

As a complementary check, the aperiodic exponent in HD-EEG was estimated using Irregular Resampling Auto-Spectral Analysis (IRASA) and compared to specparam refit in fixed mode over the same 2-40 Hz band.

```{python}
#| label: irasa-vs-specparam
#| echo: true
#| output: as-is
irasa_file = INTERIM_DIR / "irasa_vs_specparam_ch.csv"
if irasa_file.exists():
    irasa_df = pd.read_csv(irasa_file)
    pearson_r = irasa_df["exponent_sp"].corr(irasa_df["exponent_ir"], method="pearson")
    spearman_rho = irasa_df["exponent_sp"].corr(irasa_df["exponent_ir"], method="spearman")
    print(f"Per-channel correlation between specparam and IRASA exponents (2-40 Hz):")
    print(f"- Pearson correlation: r = {pearson_r:.3f}")
    print(f"- Spearman rank correlation: rho = {spearman_rho:.3f}")
else:
    print("IRASA vs specparam dataset not found.")
```

The per-channel comparison shows a very high correspondence between specparam and IRASA exponents in HD-EEG ($r = 0.88$), indicating that the two methods are capturing highly similar spectral slope dynamics when matched to the same frequency band.

![HD-EEG aperiodic exponent estimated by specparam versus IRASA (fixed model, 2-40 Hz). The dashed line marks identity.](figures/chapter2/hd_exponent_specparam_vs_irasa.svg){#fig-hd-exp-specparam-irasa}
